text: Everything you've built so far works the moment you click run in a notebook. That's not good enough for a table the Store Operations lead checks every morning — it has to be ready every morning, without anyone remembering to click anything. This lesson covers how that actually happens: a scheduled job.

Here's the shape, written out in plain English rather than any one platform's specific screens, because Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric both implement this same idea with different menus. A schedule triggers the job once a day. Land bronze runs first. Clean silver depends on land bronze finishing successfully. Aggregate gold depends on clean silver. A validation task depends on aggregate gold. And if anything in that chain fails, it alerts the on-call channel.

Three decisions matter here, not just the mechanics. The depends-on chain guarantees each task only starts after the one before it actually succeeded — without it, a scheduler might try to clean silver before bronze has finished loading that day's data at all. The trigger time, five A-M in this sketch, isn't arbitrary — it has to account for when the in-store POS export is actually guaranteed to have landed, or the whole run processes incomplete data. And the failure alert matters because a scheduled job that silently breaks is worse than no automation — the stakeholder keeps trusting a table that quietly stopped updating.

That's the orchestration concept this pipeline needs — the same shape whether you build it as an Azure Databricks job or a Microsoft Fabric pipeline. Next lesson, you'll connect Power BI to the Gold table this whole pipeline produces.
